A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same counterfactual-alignment research despite the changed title and substantial revision. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original LIDC-IDRI classification and saliency results, counterfactual visualizations, and generated radiology-report examples.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and alignment results across medical imaging datasets, component ablations, shortcut experiments, and qualitative visualizations.

M1.justification: The spatial alignment loss and implicit-gradient optimization remain. However, v2 Section 4.3 extends v1's existing attribute hierarchy with explicit attribute-space counterfactual optimization and a separate attribute-alignment loss, substantially changing the training objective and procedure. The GPT-4 report-generation interface is removed.

E1.justification: LIDC-IDRI is retained, while CBIS-DDSM mammography, BraTS brain MRI, and Aryashah2k breast ultrasound evaluations are added, including Appendix C.1. Marker and intensity shortcut scenarios expand the tested input conditions. The radiology-report generation demonstration is removed.

E2.justification: RRR/Ross, ICNN/Zhang, BagNets, CDEP/Rieger, CIDG/Chang, and Oracle remain corresponding comparators. Vanilla no longer participates in the main baseline comparison or CAM panels, although v2 Table 2 retains an unaligned ablation control. Renaming the retained methods does not constitute new baselines.

E3.justification: The stated LIDC validation/test sizes change from 244/238 to 238/244. Training changes from 300 epochs to 100 for attribute prediction and 30 for classification, with revised network configurations. v2 also introduces label-correlated training symbols randomized during validation/testing. Accuracy and saliency/CAM precision remain the evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: v2 Table 2 separately tests no alignment, spatial alignment, and hierarchical alignment, providing component analysis absent from v1. Appendix C.2 adds comparisons across absent, intensity, and +/- shortcuts. CAM and counterfactual case studies are revised and expanded, while the GPT-4 report case study is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report three seeds and display variability: error bars in v1 Figure 3 and parenthetical values in v2 Tables 1–2. No changed run count, uncertainty estimator, confidence-interval procedure, or significance test is reported; the display format changes.

E6.justification: v1 reports 81% LIDC saliency precision; v2 Table 1 reports 0.751 CAM precision under changed method/settings, so this is not a comparable performance decline. v2 adds breast CAM precision/accuracy of 0.805/0.656 and extensive modality, ablation, and shortcut results in Tables 2–4. Qualitative results are also replaced or expanded.

T1.justification: v2 adds probability-of-causation formalism, causal identification assumptions, and Propositions A.4–A.5 with proofs. Section 4.3 explicitly develops CCCE and its exogeneity/monotonicity assumptions, beyond v1's brief attribution-method reference. The existing implicit-function reasoning is retained and expanded with linear-system and conjugate-gradient derivations.

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from a general human-centered spatial alignment loss to alignment of the entire image-to-attributes-to-diagnosis causal mechanism. This hierarchical claim becomes central in v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion, alongside demonstrated utility in lung and breast diagnosis. The original loss and implicit-optimization contributions remain.

C2.justification: The causal-feature transfer explanation remains, but v2 interprets separate contributions from spatial and hierarchical alignment and identifies baseline reliance on planted shortcuts. It adds implicit-Jacobian computational expense as a limitation, while dropping v1's explicit discussion of the possible accuracy–alignment tradeoff.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access URL, dataset-specific regularization values, alignment weights, the three-attribute subset search limit, and separate network diagrams. Conversely, it omits v1's exact CT resampling/HU settings, explicit patient-level splitting statement, attribute-binarization table, and report prompt. These are substantial, mixed changes in reproducibility documentation.

R1.justification: The related-work positioning changes from broad human-centered and ante-hoc XAI taxonomies to visual alignment and medical explainability. v2 adds substantial causal, optimization, medical, and recent counterfactual literature, including Pearl, MAGI, and medical case-based explanations, while removing much of the earlier taxonomy and report-generation context.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. Methodology is reorganized into alignment loss, optimization, and hierarchical alignment; experimental sections and appendices are substantially restructured. This exceeds terminology updates or the insertion of additional results.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the introductory and method figures, adds a causal diagram and additional architecture diagram, and replaces the primary performance bar charts with tables. It adds ablation and supplementary-result tables, revises counterfactual and CAM displays, adds breast visualizations, and removes the radiology-report figure.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is stronger validation: v2's component ablations and controlled shortcut tests address v1's limited evidence about why alignment works, while the breast-diagnosis evaluation extends the single-dataset demonstration. The hierarchical objective is also substantially clearer. These gains outweigh documentation losses, although omitted preprocessing/binarization details and the sign inconsistency following Equation 4 limit reproducibility and mathematical clarity.
